title: Peace, Be Still
subtitle: Mark in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Mark begins with a voice shouting in the wilderness and a sky torn open, and then everything happens immediately: nets dropped on the shore, a fever gone, a leper touched, a storm hushed, a girl told to get up and given something to eat. His friends misunderstand, argue, fall asleep, and run. And it ends at an empty tomb, with a message for the disciples—and Peter—and three women too frightened to say a word.

This book walks through it in thirty-six short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the story touches—a net left on the shore, a cushion in a boat, a broken jar, a linen cloth on a garden path—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the Gospel of Mark alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: the voice
paintings.epigraph: “the voice of one crying in the wilderness”
paintings.poem:
no birth story here.
no star, no manger.

Mark starts
with a man in camel's hair
standing in the dry country,
eating locusts and wild honey,
shouting beside a river.

and what he shouts
is not his own name.

someone is coming,
he says,
and I'm not worthy
to bend down
and untie his sandals.

the good news begins
with a voice
that knew how to step aside.

paintings.title: torn open
paintings.epigraph: “he saw the heavens parting, and the Spirit descending on him like a dove.”
paintings.poem:
he came up
dripping from the river

and the sky
came apart.

not opened like a door.
torn,
like cloth.

and through the tear,
a voice:

you are my beloved Son.
I am well pleased.

he hadn't preached yet.
hadn't healed anyone.
hadn't done one thing
worth writing down.

the pleasure
came first.

paintings.title: immediately
paintings.epigraph: “Immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.”
paintings.poem:
Mark's favorite word
is immediately.

up from the water, immediately.
into the desert, immediately.
nets dropped, fever gone,
the news running ahead,
immediately.

a gospel
in a hurry.

but see where
the hurry went first:

forty days
among the wild animals,
with angels serving him.

even the fastest story
begins in the wilderness.

paintings.title: fishers
paintings.epigraph: “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.”
paintings.poem:
two brothers throwing a net.
two more mending one.

come after me.

and the nets
went slack on the water.

their father stayed in the boat
with the hired men,
watching his sons
walk up the shore.

following cost something
from the very first page.

and the hands
that let go of the nets
would one day
hand out bread
to five thousand.

paintings.title: by the hand
paintings.epigraph: “He came and took her by the hand, and raised her up.”
paintings.poem:
Simon's mother-in-law
lay sick with a fever.

he came,
took her by the hand,
and raised her up.

the fever left
immediately,
and she served them.

healing, in Mark,
doesn't look like fireworks.

it looks like a woman
back on her feet
in her own house,
passing bread to her guests.

paintings.title: a deserted place
paintings.epigraph: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out”
paintings.poem:
the whole town
had crowded his door
the night before.

so he got up
while it was still dark
and walked out
to where no one was,

and prayed.

his friends went hunting for him.
everyone is looking for you!

he knew.
that's why he'd gone.

some mornings
you have to be found
by God
before anyone else
can find you.

paintings.title: I want to
paintings.epigraph: “Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him”
paintings.poem:
if you want to,
you can.

he wasn't asking
whether Jesus was able.

he was asking
whether he was wanted.

and Jesus,
moved with compassion,
did the one thing
everyone had learned
not to do.

he touched him.

then he answered
the real question:

I want to.

paintings.title: the tax office
paintings.epigraph: “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick.”
paintings.poem:
Levi sat
where everyone could see him
and no one wanted to.

follow me.

he got up
and left the coins on the table.

that night his house was full
of tax collectors and sinners,
and Jesus right in the middle,
eating.

a doctor goes
where the sick are,
and sits down,
and stays for supper.

paintings.title: with him
paintings.epigraph: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him”
paintings.poem:
before the preaching,
before any of it,
he chose twelve
that they might be
with him.

fishermen.
a tax collector.
a zealot.
and Judas,
right there on the list.

Mark will show them
arguing,
falling asleep,
running.

but the first job
was never to be impressive.

it was to stay close.

paintings.title: while he sleeps
paintings.epigraph: “first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”
paintings.poem:
a farmer scatters seed
and goes to bed.

gets up.
goes to bed.
gets up.

and the seed grows
while he isn't looking,
and he doesn't know how.

first the blade.
then the ear.
then the full grain.

you can water.
you can wait.
you can't make it hurry.

the kingdom
keeps growing
in the dark,
while you sleep.

paintings.title: the cushion
paintings.epigraph: “Peace! Be still!”
paintings.poem:
Mark remembers the cushion,
in the stern,
under a sleeping head,
while the boat filled with water.

teacher,
don't you care
that we are dying?

he got up
and spoke to the sea
the way you'd hush a room:

peace. be still.

and there was a great calm,
and they were more afraid
in the quiet
than in the storm.

paintings.title: clothed
paintings.epigraph: “sitting, clothed, and in his right mind”
paintings.poem:
he lived among the tombs.
they'd tried chains.
no one could hold him.

then a boat came in
from across the sea.

and the town came out
and found him
sitting.
clothed.
in his right mind.

and they were afraid.

go home, Jesus told him.
tell them how the Lord
had mercy on you.

and he went through ten cities
telling it.

paintings.title: all the truth
paintings.epigraph: “came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth.”
paintings.poem:
she was already healed.
she could have slipped away.

but he stopped the crowd:
who touched my clothes?

so she came forward,
shaking,
and told him
all the truth.

twelve years of it.
every doctor.
every coin.

he had already
healed her body.

now he wanted
the rest of her.

paintings.title: only believe
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t be afraid, only believe.”
paintings.poem:
he had waited
while Jesus stopped
for someone else.

then word came from his house:
your daughter is dead.
why bother the teacher?

and Jesus turned to him:
don't be afraid.
only believe.

not believe harder.
not believe everything.
only.

when every other word
is taken from you,
this one is still small enough
to carry home.

paintings.title: something to eat
paintings.epigraph: “Girl, I tell you, get up!”
paintings.poem:
they laughed at him
when he said she was only asleep.

he sent them out,
took her hand,
and said it the way you'd wake a child
in the morning:

talitha cumi.
little girl, get up.

and she got up and walked.

then the Lord of life
turned to her parents:

give her something to eat.

paintings.title: the carpenter
paintings.epigraph: “Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary”
paintings.poem:
back home
they knew him too well.

the carpenter.
Mary's son.
we know his brothers.
his sisters live right here.

and they were offended.

Mark says it plainly:
he could do no mighty work there,
except a few sick people
healed under his hands.

and he marveled
at their unbelief.

sometimes the hardest place
to be seen clearly
is the place
that watched you grow up.

paintings.title: rest awhile
paintings.epigraph: “Y ou come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.”
paintings.poem:
so many coming and going
they had no time to eat.

come away, he said.
rest awhile.

so they rowed to an empty place,
and the crowd ran around the shore
and got there first.

he looked at them,
sheep without a shepherd,
and had compassion,
and began to teach.

he knew what it was
to be tired
and give anyway.

paintings.title: green grass
paintings.epigraph: “He commanded them that everyone should sit down in groups on the green grass.”
paintings.poem:
you give them something to eat.
with what?
go and see.

five loaves.
two fish.

he had them sit down in groups
on the green grass,
like beds in a garden,

and he looked up, blessed, broke,
and kept handing it along.

a strange thing to remember,
the color of the grass—

unless you were there,
sitting in it,
full.

paintings.title: crumbs
paintings.epigraph: “Y et even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
paintings.poem:
she wasn't from Israel,
and her little girl was suffering.

his first answer
sounded like a closed door.

but she kept her hand on the latch:
yes, Lord.
but even the dogs under the table
eat the children's crumbs.

she wasn't asking for the loaf.
she knew how much bread
falls from a table like his.

and she went home
and found her daughter
lying on the bed,
free.

paintings.title: be opened
paintings.epigraph: “Looking up to heaven, he sighed”
paintings.poem:
he took the man aside,
away from the crowd.

he looked up to heaven
and sighed.

not a speech.
a sigh,
as if he felt
the weight of all that silence.

ephphatha.
be opened.

and he heard,
and he spoke clearly.

sometimes the prayer
that opens everything
is only a breath.

paintings.title: trees walking
paintings.epigraph: “I see men; for I see them like trees walking.”
paintings.poem:
do you see anything?

people, the man said.
but they look like trees,
walking.

halfway.

Jesus didn't scold him.
he laid his hands on his eyes
again,

and the man looked hard,
and saw everyone clearly.

if you only see
in blurs so far,
say so.

he doesn't mind
touching you twice.

paintings.title: who do you say
paintings.epigraph: “But who do you say that I am?”
paintings.poem:
Peter got it right.
you are the Christ.

and moments later
got it completely wrong.

when Jesus spoke of suffering,
Peter took him aside
to correct him.

Mark tells it straight:
the same mouth,
the same road,
the right answer
and the wrong one.

get behind me,
Jesus said.

which is also,
if you think about it,
where followers walk.

paintings.title: help my unbelief
paintings.epigraph: “I believe. Help my unbelief!”
paintings.poem:
if you can do anything,
the father said.

if you can?
all things are possible
to the one who believes.

and the father cried out
with tears:
I believe.
help my unbelief.

half faith, half fear,
both said out loud.

it was enough.

a hand took the boy's,
and he stood up.

paintings.title: in the middle
paintings.epigraph: “He took a little child, and set him in the middle of them.”
paintings.poem:
what were you arguing about
on the road?

silence.
they'd been arguing
about who was the greatest.

he set a small child
in the middle of them,
and took the child in his arms.

if you want to be first,
be last,
be everyone's servant—

and start
with the smallest one
in the room.

paintings.title: loved him
paintings.epigraph: “Jesus looking at him loved him”
paintings.poem:
he ran up,
knelt in the road.
what must I do?

and Mark tells us,
before anything else,
Jesus looked at him
and loved him.

then the hard word:
one thing you lack.
sell it. give it away.
come, follow me.

and he went away sad,
for he had so much.

the love came first.
the hard word
was the love, speaking.

paintings.title: right and left
paintings.epigraph: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve”
paintings.poem:
James and John
asked for the best seats,
one on his right,
one on his left.

can you drink my cup?
we can!

the Son of Man, he told them,
came not to be served
but to serve,
and to give his life
for many.

they wanted the places
beside a throne.

when the time came,
the places on his right and left
were two crosses.

paintings.title: the cloak
paintings.epigraph: “He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.”
paintings.poem:
son of David,
have mercy on me!

be quiet, they said.
he shouted louder.

and Jesus stood still.
call him.

so Bartimaeus
threw off his cloak,
maybe all he had,
and sprang up,
still blind,
toward a voice.

what do you want?
to see again.

and the first road he saw,
he followed him on.

paintings.title: the Lord needs him
paintings.epigraph: “The Lord needs him”
paintings.poem:
a young colt
tied by a door.
no one had ever sat on him.

what are you doing?
the Lord needs him.

and that was enough.

just a borrowed animal,
tied up, waiting,
with a place in the story
he knew nothing about.

you may be tied to a doorpost
somewhere, waiting.

he knows the street.
he knows the door.

paintings.title: he sat and watched
paintings.epigraph: “she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.”
paintings.poem:
he sat down
across from the offering box
and watched.

rich people.
heavy handfuls.

one widow.
two small coins.

he's still watching.

not how much.
how much is left.

paintings.title: broken open
paintings.epigraph: “She broke the jar, and poured it over his head.”
paintings.poem:
she didn't pour a little
and save the rest.
she broke the jar.

there's no closing it
after that.

what a waste,
someone muttered.

leave her alone.
she has done what she could.
she has anointed my body
for the burying.

wherever the good news goes,
he said,
her story will go too.

and here it is.

paintings.title: Abba
paintings.epigraph: “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you.”
paintings.poem:
he had told a father,
all things are possible.

now, fallen on the ground,
he said it himself:

Abba.
all things are possible to you.
take this cup away from me.

and then,
still holding on to Abba,
not what I want.
what you want.

a little way off,
his friends were sleeping.

he prayed the hardest prayer alone,
and still called God
by the closest name.

paintings.title: the linen cloth
paintings.epigraph: “he left the linen cloth, and fled”
paintings.poem:
they all left him and fled.
Mark says it plainly.
all.

then one more:
a young man
wrapped only in a linen cloth,
who slipped out of it
when they grabbed at him
and ran into the dark.

the next time Mark mentions linen,
it will be wrapped around Jesus.

the next young man we meet
will be sitting in the tomb
in white,
not running at all.

paintings.title: the second crow
paintings.epigraph: “When he thought about that, he wept.”
paintings.poem:
he followed at a distance,
all the way into the courtyard—
farther than the others went.

a servant girl:
you were with him.

I don't know this man.
once, twice, three times.

the rooster crowed the second time,
and Peter remembered.

Mark doesn't dress it up:
when he thought about that,
he wept.

keep that picture.
you'll need it
at the empty tomb.

paintings.title: truly
paintings.epigraph: “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
paintings.poem:
at the beginning of the book
the sky was torn open.

now,
as Jesus breathed his last,
the temple curtain
tore in two,
from the top
to the bottom.

torn from heaven's side.

and the first human voice in Mark
to say it out loud—
this man was the Son of God—

wasn't one of the twelve.
they were gone.

it was the soldier
standing opposite him,
who watched
how he died.

paintings.title: and Peter
paintings.epigraph: “go, tell his disciples and Peter”
paintings.poem:
he has risen.
he is not here.

then the message,
with two words
no one else would have added:

go, tell his disciples—
and Peter.

the one who swore
he didn't know the man.
the one who wept by the fire.

named.
on purpose.

he is going ahead of you
into Galilee.
there you will see him.

paintings.title: for they were afraid
paintings.epigraph: “They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.”
paintings.poem:
many of the oldest copies of Mark
end right here:

they said nothing to anyone,
for they were afraid.

no bow on it.
just three women,
hearts pounding,
holding the biggest news in the world
in their mouths.

but you know.
you've heard.

so somewhere, after the trembling,
somebody spoke.

the story doesn't end
with the silence.
it ends with whoever
tells it next.
